title: Andalucía: Ronda, the Alpujarras & Cabo de Gata
subRegion: Andalucía — Serranía de Ronda, Sierra Nevada's southern slope and Almería

bestPeriod.avoid: July–August (Sevilla-side inland temperatures over 42°C, coastal traffic); December–February for Puerto de la Ragua snow closures

accommodation.note: Ronda parador-adjacent, an Alpujarra cortijo, Cabo de Gata

food.note: Menú del día €14–€18; Granada tapas come free with drinks

transport.note: Rental, fuel (~€1.60/l), minimal tolls, city parking

profile.difficultyNote: 2 — driving-led, with a 2 h Torcal karst loop and a stepped 1 h in Ronda's gorge

gatewayAirport: AGP — Málaga Costa del Sol; 100 km / 1 h 40 to Ronda via the A-357 and A-367, or 1 h 25 on the A-397
summary: Andalucía has more good driving roads than any other region in Spain, and this loop links three completely different ones: the cliff-edge A-397 up from the coast to Ronda, the ledge road through the Alpujarras that Gerald Brenan wrote about, and the empty desert straights of Almería. In between you climb Puerto de la Ragua at 2,000 m over the eastern shoulder of the Sierra Nevada — a crossing that goes from Moorish terraces to alpine pine to lunar badlands in ninety minutes. The week ends in the volcanic coves of Cabo de Gata, the driest place in Europe, where the roads are wide, empty and the light in October is extraordinary. It suits drivers who want variety of terrain and can navigate Spain's expanding low-emission zones without collecting fines.

itinerary.title: Málaga to Ronda by the cliff road
itinerary.morning: Collect the car at AGP. Head west on the A-7 to San Pedro de Alcántara — 55 km of coastal sprawl, but it is the price of admission to the A-397.
itinerary.afternoon: The A-397 climbs 1,000 m in 49 km with the Mediterranean falling away behind. Stop at the Puerto del Madroño layby for the view back to Gibraltar and, on a clear day, the Rif. Arrive Ronda mid-afternoon and park in the Martínez Astein or Socorro underground lots.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Puente Nuevo at sunset — the 98 m bridge over the El Tajo gorge is best from the Mirador de Aldehuela on the north side, or from the Jardines de Cuenca below. Dinner at Tragatá, Benito Gómez's tapas bar.
itinerary.dayStats: 105 km / 2 h; A-397 climbs to 950 m; AP-7 avoided; Ronda garage €14–€18/day.
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Montelirio, Ronda — a clifftop 18th-century mansion with valet parking.

itinerary.title: Grazalema, the white villages and El Torcal
itinerary.morning: West on the A-372 into the Sierra de Grazalema, over the Puerto del Boyar at 1,103 m, and down to Grazalema village. Continue to Zahara de la Sierra for the reservoir view, then the CA-9104 over the Puerto de las Palomas — 1,357 m, and one of the great white-village panoramas.
itinerary.afternoon: Return east and cross to **El Torcal de Antequera**. The upper car park is accessed by a narrow 4 km road with a barrier system in high season — arrive before 11:00 or park at the lower lot and take the shuttle. Walk the Ruta Amarilla (2.9 km) through the karst pinnacles.
itinerary.evening: Drive to Antequera and eat at Arte de Cozina for porra antequerana. Or return to Ronda if you prefer one base.
itinerary.dayStats: 210 km / 4 h with stops; Puerto del Boyar 1,103 m; Puerto de las Palomas 1,357 m; El Torcal free entry, parking €2.
itinerary.sleep: Parador de Antequera, or return to Hotel Montelirio, Ronda.

itinerary.title: Across to Granada and the Alhambra
itinerary.morning: The A-92 east from Antequera is fast, free dual carriageway through olive country. Two hours to Granada.
itinerary.afternoon: **Do not drive into central Granada.** The ZBE covers the historic core. Park at the Alhambra's own visitor car park (€6/day) or the Parking San Agustín, and use taxis or the C30/C32 microbuses thereafter. Your Alhambra ticket carries a strict half-hour entry slot for the **Nasrid Palaces** — miss it and it is void.
itinerary.evening: Sunset from the Mirador de San Nicolás in the Albaicín — go 40 minutes before sunset for a spot on the wall. Then free tapas crawl on Calle Navas: Los Diamantes for fried fish, Bodegas Castañeda for the classics.
itinerary.dayStats: 100 km / 1 h 40; A-92 toll-free; Alhambra €19 general, Nasrid Palaces timed entry; Granada ZBE camera-enforced.
itinerary.sleep: Hotel Casa 1800 Granada (Albaicín, arranges permitted access and a garage) or Alhambra Palace.

itinerary.title: The Alpujarra ledge road
itinerary.morning: Leave Granada south on the A-44, exit at Lanjarón and pick up the A-348 / A-4132. Órgiva is the last big fuel stop. Then the Poqueira gorge: Pampaneira, Bubión and Capileira stacked on the mountainside, all with lower car parks and lanes too tight to drive.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue east to **Trevélez** at 1,476 m — Spain's ham-curing village, where the jamón is air-dried at altitude. The road beyond, through Juviles and Bérchules to Cádiar, is the quietest and best-surfaced section of the whole Alpujarra.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at Mesón La Fragua in Trevélez, or at your cortijo. The night sky here is exceptional — the Sierra Nevada blocks the coastal light dome.
itinerary.dayStats: 120 km / 3 h 15 with village stops; road runs 700–1,600 m; Trevélez 1,476 m; last supermarket fuel at Órgiva.
itinerary.sleep: Hotel La Fragua II, Trevélez, or Alquería de Morayma near Cádiar — both have their own parking.

itinerary.title: Puerto de la Ragua, Tabernas and the desert coast
itinerary.morning: Climb the A-337 from Laroles to **Puerto de la Ragua at 2,000 m** — 15 km of steady, narrow, well-graded ascent through pine into open moorland at the col. There is a small refuge, a picnic area and a nordic ski trailhead. Descend the north side to La Calahorra, whose Renaissance castle sits on a bare hill above the Marquesado plain.
itinerary.afternoon: East on the A-92 through Guadix's cave-house quarter, then into the **Tabernas desert** — Europe's only true desert, and the backdrop to A Fistful of Dollars. Fort Bravo / Texas Hollywood is the surviving film set worth stopping at.
itinerary.evening: Drop south to Cabo de Gata. Dinner at La Ola in San José for grilled red prawns.
itinerary.dayStats: 230 km / 5 h; Puerto de la Ragua 2,000 m, snow-closed in spells December–March; A-92 free; Tabernas gets to 42°C in summer.
itinerary.sleep: MC San José or Cortijo El Sotillo, San José — both with secure lots, which matters here.

itinerary.title: Rodalquilar, Las Negras and the cove roads
itinerary.morning: Drive north to **Rodalquilar**, an abandoned gold-mining village in a volcanic amphitheatre with the mill ruins standing open to walk through. Then over to **Las Negras**, a whitewashed fishing hamlet at the end of a long straight road.
itinerary.afternoon: The Playa de los Muertos car park is on the AL-5106 above the beach; the descent is a 20-minute rough path. Alternatively, the **Playa de Mónsul and Playa de los Genoveses** track south of San José is **closed to private cars in summer** — a shuttle bus runs from San José and the barrier is enforced. Out of season you can drive the piste, which is graded gravel and fine for a normal car.
itinerary.evening: Sunset from the **Mirador de la Amatista** on the AL-3115 between Rodalquilar and La Isleta — the best coastal viewpoint in the park, and it faces the right way for the last hour of light.
itinerary.dayStats: 85 km / 2 h; Mónsul/Genoveses track 7 km gravel, seasonal vehicle ban; shuttle €5 return; park entry free.
itinerary.sleep: MC San José or Cortijo El Sotillo (second night).

itinerary.title: The coast road back to Málaga
itinerary.morning: Head west on the A-7 along the Almería and Granada coast. The stretch through the Sierra de Gádor and the Salobreña plain is a series of viaducts and tunnels with genuine sea views. Stop at Salobreña's castle above the sugar-cane fields.
itinerary.afternoon: Optional detour to Nerja for the caves, or straight through to Málaga. Return the car at AGP — refuel at the Cepsa on the A-7 approach, not at the airport.
itinerary.evening: If you have hours to spare, park at the Muelle Uno garage and walk Málaga's centre — Picasso Museum, the Alcazaba, and the roof terrace at AC Málaga Palacio.
itinerary.dayStats: 220 km / 2 h 45; A-7 toll-free (AP-7 optional, €3–€9 per section); Málaga ZBE — use Muelle Uno or Alcazaba garages.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Montelirio
accommodationStrategy.description: Built into the cliff edge beside the Puente Nuevo, with a valet service that removes the problem of Ronda's near-impossible old-town parking. Terrace rooms look straight down the El Tajo gorge, and it is 60 seconds' walk from the bridge, so you can shoot the blue hour without moving the car. €150–€230.

accommodationStrategy.name: Alquería de Morayma
accommodationStrategy.description: A working farm estate on the eastern Alpujarra with its own wine, olive oil and generous open parking — useful, because every other Alpujarra village has none. It sits at the base of the A-337, meaning the Puerto de la Ragua climb starts 15 minutes after breakfast rather than an hour. €90–€130.

accommodationStrategy.name: Cortijo El Sotillo
accommodationStrategy.description: Just outside San José with a large gated car park, which is the practical point: San José's street parking is metered, contested and the Genoveses shuttle leaves from the village. Stables, a pool for the flat afternoon hours, and a five-minute walk to the harbour restaurants. €120–€190.

logistics.connectivity: Spain is in the EU roaming zone. Coverage is good almost everywhere including the Alpujarra villages; the exceptions are the Puerto de la Ragua col and the interior of Cabo de Gata's tracks. Download offline maps for the park.
logistics.emergency: 112 across Spain. Guardia Civil 062; mountain rescue in the Sierra Nevada is run by the Guardia Civil's GREIM via 112. Road assistance is through your rental's own number — RACE is 900 100 992.
logistics.weather: The **terral**, a hot dry offshore wind, can push Málaga past 40°C for days in summer. Grazalema records Spain's highest rainfall and produces dense fog on the A-372 with little warning. Cabo de Gata is genuinely arid — under 200 mm of rain a year — but a **levante** easterly makes the eastern coves unswimmable and blows fine grit.
logistics.bookingWindows: **The Alhambra is the hard constraint** — tickets go on sale up to three months ahead on alhambra-patronato.es and the Nasrid Palaces slots sell out weeks in advance for April–October. Buy from the official site only; resellers charge triple. Cabo de Gata accommodation books out for August and Semana Santa.
logistics.money: Euro. Cards work everywhere including village bars and fuel pumps. Keep €20 in coins for blue-zone street meters. Tipping is minimal: rounding up, or 5% for a full dinner. Granada is one of the last cities where a drink comes with a free tapa.
logistics.transportRules: No vignette. Motorway tolls are limited to the AP-7 Costa del Sol on this route. Speed limits are 120 on autovías, 90 on conventional roads, 30 in most urban single-lane streets. Speed cameras are frequent and signed; radar detectors are illegal. Two warning triangles were replaced by the mandatory **V-16 connected beacon from 1 January 2026** — confirm your rental has one. Alcohol limit 0.05% (0.03% for drivers under two years).
logistics.permits: Cabo de Gata-Níjar is a natural park: the Genoveses and Mónsul access track is closed to private vehicles in high season with a paid shuttle instead, and wild camping and campervan overnighting are prohibited and actively fined. Drones require registration and are banned over the park and over the Alhambra. Sierra Nevada National Park restricts vehicle access above certain points on the Hoya de la Mora road.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable throughout, though Almería's is very hard and most people buy bottled. Heatstroke is the real risk in Tabernas and at El Torcal — go early, carry water. Sea urchins and occasional Portuguese man o' war after easterly winds on the Almería coast. Puerto de la Ragua at 2,000 m needs no acclimatisation but can be 15°C colder than the coast.

proTips: Buy the Alhambra ticket the day it opens for your month, and choose a **Nasrid Palaces slot before 09:00 or after 18:00**. The half-hour entry window is enforced to the minute, and midday slots put you in the Court of the Lions with 400 other people.
Drive the A-397 **upward from the coast**, not down. The sea views open behind you on the ascent and you are on the inside of the drops; descending it puts you on the cliff edge for 49 km.

Park outside every ZBE. In Granada use the Alhambra visitor lot or Parking San Agustín; in Málaga use Muelle Uno. Camera-enforced ZBE fines are €200 and arrive via the rental company months later with an admin fee on top.

Check the Puerto de la Ragua before committing on Day 5. There is no barrier and no live feed — the Junta de Andalucía's traffic information and the Laroles village bar are both better sources than any app.
Reach El Torcal's upper car park before 11:00. In peak season a barrier system diverts arrivals to the lower lot and a shuttle, adding an hour to a two-hour walk.

The Genoveses and Mónsul beach track is closed to cars in summer. If you visit in October or April you can drive the gravel piste yourself — a normal hatchback handles it at 20 km/h, and you get Spain's best beach with a dozen people on it.

Shoot the Alpujarra villages from the road **below** Pampaneira in the late afternoon; the classic stacked-white-village shot only works when the western sun is on the terraces. Mornings there are entirely in shadow.
Trevélez's ham cellars offer free tastings and will vacuum-pack for travel. A whole leg is not hand-luggage; a sliced 100 g pack is, and it is a fifth of the price of the same ham in Málaga.

Confirm your rental carries the V-16 emergency beacon rather than triangles. Since January 2026 the beacon is the legal requirement, and standing on a hard shoulder placing triangles is now both illegal and dangerous.

raw.Total distance: ~1,000 km over 7 days. Longest leg is Day 5, Granada–Cabo de Gata via the full Alpujarra road and Puerto de la Ragua, 230 km in a genuine 5 h.
raw.A-397 (San Pedro de Alcántara–Ronda), 49: the famous one. Climbs from sea level to 1,000 m over the Serranía de Ronda with sweeping engineered curves, a 950 m summit near Puerto del Madroño, and long unguarded drops. Excellent surface, no toll, but it is a favourite of motorcyclists and Guardia Civil speed patrols in equal measure. Allow 1 h 10, not 50 minutes.
raw.A-372 (Ronda–Grazalema–El Bosque), 52 km: narrower and more technical than the A-397, threading the Sierra de Grazalema — the wettest place in Spain, which means fog and wet limestone even in May. Puerto del Boyar at 1,103 m has a proper viewpoint layby.
raw.A-4132 Alpujarra road (Lanjarón–Órgiva–P: roughly 90 km of continuous contour-hugging two-lane road at 700–1,600 m, with the Poqueira gorge villages (Pampaneira, Bubión, Capileira) stacked above it. Trevélez at 1,476 m is among the highest villages in Spain. Village streets are one-car-wide with 90° turns — park at the lower lots.
raw.Puerto de la Ragua (A-337), 2,000 m: the only paved crossing of the Sierra Nevada's eastern end, linking the Alpujarra to the Marquesado plain and Guadix. Narrow, well-surfaced, ~15 km of climb from La Calahorra, with a cross-country ski centre at the col. **Closes on snow, typically for spells between December and March**, and there is no live barrier — check before committing.
raw.Tolls: Andalucía is almost entirely toll-free. The **AP-7 Málaga–Estepona (AP-7 Costa del Sol)** is the exception, costing roughly €3–€9 per section and up to ~€12 in high season for the full Málaga–Guadiaro run; the parallel free A-7 is slower and busier. The AP-4 Sevilla–Cádiz became toll-free in 2019. No vignette exists in Spain.
raw.Low-emission zones (ZBE): the item most likely to cost you money. **Málaga's ZBE** covers the centre and is camera-enforced; **Granada's ZBE** covers the historic core including the Realejo and much of the Albaicín approach. Rental cars registered in Spain carry a DGT environmental sticker (etiqueta ambiental) — a modern petrol car gets a "C" label which is currently admitted in both, but non-resident and unregistered vehicles are not automatically exempt. The safe practice is to park in a designated underground car park outside the zone and walk.
raw.Car rental & cross-border: Málaga is one of Europe's cheapest rental markets, which is also why the counter upsell is aggressive — decline the fuel-purchase option and take a card with a large enough limit for the excess hold. Gibraltar is permitted by most companies but frequently requires declaration; Morocco is refused by nearly all. Cross into Portugal is generally free of charge on Spanish rentals. One-way AGP-to-Almería drops are €60–€120.
raw.Fuel & hazards: fuel is plentiful except on the Alpujarra road above Órgiva (fill at Órgiva) and across Puerto de la Ragua (fill at Cádiar or Guadix). Hazards: goats and Iberian ibex on the A-4132 at dawn and dusk, fog banks in Grazalema, and the fact that Andalucian villages have unmarked speed bumps that will destroy a low rental's sump.

sources.verified: Málaga and Granada both operate camera-enforced ZBE low-emission zones covering their historic centres, with the DGT environmental sticker system determining access; Spain has no vignette and Andalucía is largely toll-free apart from the AP-7 Costa del Sol; Puerto de la Ragua's altitude (~2,000 m) and its status as the paved crossing of the eastern Sierra Nevada, subject to snow closure.
sources.confidenceNotes: ZBE rules are the most volatile element — Spanish municipalities have been phasing in enforcement on different timetables and the treatment of foreign-plated and non-resident vehicles differs between Málaga and Granada; re-verify against each ayuntamiento's own page before publishing. Puerto de la Ragua has no fixed closure dates and no live status feed; the December–March window is typical, not guaranteed. AP-7 Costa del Sol section prices vary seasonally and should be re-quoted. Alhambra ticket pricing and the three-month sales window are revised periodically. The Genoveses/Mónsul vehicle restriction dates are set annually by the park authority. The V-16 beacon requirement took effect 1 January 2026 — confirm rental fleet compliance.
